### **Research questions**

*Linear regression:* Can we predict how much someone trusts politicians based on their education, age, political interest and income?

### **Data pre-processing**

```{r}
#| output: false

# setup R library's and working directories
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

# Define variables pointing to the relevant directories
dataDir <- "data"
outDir <- "output"
figDir <- "figures"
```

#### **Changing names**

```{r}
# Read csv and store it in the data variable. 
full_data <- read.csv(here::here(dataDir, "ESS11e04_2.csv"))

```

Current size of the data-set: `{r} nrow(full_data)` rows and `{r} ncol(full_data)` columns.

```{r}
# Select the columns we will need and store it in a new table based on the codebook.
df <- select(full_data, trstplt, agea, eisced, hinctnta, polintr)

# Rename columns so the names are more readable based on the codebook
df <- rename(df, 
			 age                  = agea,
		   trust.in.politicians = trstplt,
			 education            = eisced, 
			 household.income     = hinctnta, 
			 political.interest   = polintr,
			 )
```

#### **NA Encoding**

| Missing Value Encoding | Meaning of Encoding       |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| 0                      | Not possible to harmonize |
| 55                     | Other                     |
| 66                     | Not applicable            |
| 7, 77                  | Refusal of Answer         |
| 8, 88                  | Don't know                |
| 9, 99, 999             | Missing Value             |

The data set contains several codes that represent responses that do not represent meaningful values for our analysis. We will re-code them as missing values

For trust.in.politicians, household.income and education the values we re-code are: 55, 66, 77, 88 and 99.

```{r}
filter_values <- c(55, 66, 77, 88, 99) 

df <- df |>
	mutate(
		trust.in.politicians = replace(
			trust.in.politicians,
			trust.in.politicians %in% filter_values,
			NA
		),
		household.income = replace(
			household.income,
			household.income %in% filter_values,
			NA
		),
		education = replace(
			education,
			education %in% filter_values,
			NA
		)
	)

```

For political.interest the values we re-code are: 7, 8 and 9.

```{r}
filter_values = c(7, 8 , 9)

df <- df |> 
	mutate(
		political.interest = replace(
			political.interest,
			political.interest %in% filter_values,
			NA
		)
	)

```

For age the value we re-code is 999, and education: 0.

```{r}
df <- df |> 
	mutate(
		age = replace(
			age,
			age == 999,
			NA
		),
		education = replace(
			education,
			education == 0,
			NA
		)
	)
```

#### **Reverse Encoding**

For easier interpretation we want all the values to be increasing. in our model. So a 0 or 1 should indicate a low value and 10 or 100 a high value. In the variable political.interest this is reversed, so we will match it with our other variables.

```{r}
df <- df |>
	mutate(
		political.interest = 5 - political.interest
	)
```

Current size of the data-set after selection: `{r} nrow(df)` rows and `{r} ncol(df)` columns.

## Explorative Data Analysis

Note: We take the assumption that variables trust.in.politicians, education, household.income and political.interest are evenly spaced. Even though the original variables are ordinal. Do we keep them numeric? switch them to ordinal? For linear Regression use numeric, but also add Spearman correlations and frequency tables to our data analysis?

#### Education

education is measured using the EISCED variable, which classifies respondents into ordered categories. A frequency table was used to examine the distribution.

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(x = education)) +
	geom_histogram() +
	labs(x = "Education level (EISCED)",
			 y = "Frequency",
			 title = "Education level frequency table") +
	stat_bin(binwidth = 0.5) +
	theme_minimal()
```

The results show that category 4 is the most represented and category 1 the least represented.

Next we calculated the mean trust in politicians per education level, as shown in the boxplot and table below.

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(education), y = trust.in.politicians)) +
	geom_boxplot() +
	labs(
		title = "Trust in Politicians by Education Level",
		x = "Education level (EISCED)",
		y = "Trust in politicians (0–10)"
	) +
	theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
df |>
	group_by(education) |>
	summarise(
		n = n(),
		mean_trust = mean(trust.in.politicians, na.rm = TRUE),
		sd_trust = sd(trust.in.politicians, na.rm = TRUE)
	)

```

We can see that the lowest education level had also the lowest mean trust. The highest education level had the highest mean trust. Standard deviations remained relatively the same. The results suggest a slight increase in mean trust in politicians as education increases.
